report:
PASS for the precise supporting theorem, including the stronger exceptional-divisor bound. The determinant estimate and the analytic Jacobian-to-multiplier inclusion are sound. No discrepancy estimate or special Fujita theorem is imported.

The external background is verified in the analytic category. Premise 0 is supported by [Bierstone–Milman, Desingularization Algorithms I](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0207098), §§1.3–1.4 and Example 1.19(1): its category explicitly includes analytic spaces, and its relatively compact scope suffices after shrinking locally. Premise 1 is supported by [Demailly, Analytic Methods in Algebraic Geometry](https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/manuscripts/analmeth_book.pdf), Definition 5.4, Proposition 5.7, Proposition 5.8 and Remark 5.9. These are local analytic statements; their multiplier transformation formula does not require projectivity or a global Kähler form. Premise 2 is supported by [Lejeune-Jalabert–Teissier](https://numdam.org/item/10.5802/afst.1203.pdf), Proposition 3.2 and §§4.1–4.2, concerning the actual normalized analytic blowup. Premises 3–5 are established in [Demailly, Complex Analytic and Differential Geometry](https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/manuscripts/agbook.pdf), Chapter II, Theorems 5.3, 7.6, 2.10 and 8.8, respectively.

Here is an independent reconstruction of the determinant argument. The analytic Rees algebra is a quotient of O_U[T_0,…,T_N], yielding a closed embedding of the ordinary blowup in U×P^N. On T_0≠0 its ambient coordinates are the base coordinates and generator ratios; the relations give f_j=f_0r_j and make the pulled-back ideal principal. Choose such a chart meeting a general point of E. Then f_0 generates the ideal there and has order m.

Restrict the finite normalization map to E and compose with this chart embedding. On the smooth locus of E this holomorphic map has finite fibers. If its maximum differential rank were r<n−1, the holomorphic constant-rank theorem on its maximum-rank open set would produce positive-dimensional local fibers, a contradiction. Thus the base coordinates and ratios restrict to differential rank n−1 on a dense open subset of E. This establishes the required rank without any assumption about the normal line.

Select n−1 corresponding functions u_i with independent restricted differentials. At a general smooth point of Y and E, write p*f_0=s^m h with h a unit. The coefficient of ds∧du_1∧…∧du_{n−1}, after division by s^{m−1}, restricts to the nonzero coefficient m h on E. Consequently this wedge has exact order m−1; the s^m dh term cannot cancel its leading term. The same argument covers n=1 with an empty tangent wedge.

Let ell=v(Jac_1(b)). Every coefficient of df_0 has valuation at least ell. Since v(f_j)≥m, the coefficients of d(f_j/f_0) have valuation at least ell−m. Coordinate differentials also meet this bound because ell≤m. Therefore, writing the base wedge as A dx_1∧…∧dx_n gives v(A)≥ell+(n−1)(ell−m)=m−n(m−ell). Pullback yields the exact identity m−1=v(A)+k_E, hence k_E+1≤n(m−ell). All comparisons occur on the smooth generic locus; no Q-Gorenstein property of Y is used.

The multiplier step also checks independently. The chain rule and d(af)=a df+f da establish coordinate and generator independence of Jac_1. The analytic multiplier formula follows from change of variables: on a normal-crossing resolution, the local integrand has factors |s_i|^{2(v_{P_i}(h)+b_i−q_i)}. Integrability requires each exponent to exceed −2, which, because these orders are integral, is exactly v_{P_i}(h)≥q_i−b_i. Properness permits checking over the fiber using finitely many local neighborhoods. Also b_i≥0 because the resolution Jacobian is holomorphic.

For a contributing divisor P, q−b_P>0 implies q>0, so its analytic center W lies in V(b). Because b has no divisorial factor, c=codim W≥2. Choose coordinates adapted to a general smooth point of W. Every generator pulls back as s^q h_j, and each of the c center coordinates as s h_i; these h-functions need not be units. In df_j∧∧_{i≠l}dx_i there are at least c−1 center-coordinate factors. At most one factor can contribute ds. A df_j normal term has order q−1, its tangent terms have order at least q, and center-coordinate tangent terms have order at least one. Thus the wedge has order at least q+c−2≥q. If l is outside the center-coordinate set, the count is even stronger. Its order is v_P(∂f_j/∂x_l)+b_P, proving the required multiplier inequality. Noncontributing divisors impose an automatic inequality. Generators themselves belong to J(b), directly because their defining integrands are bounded. Hence Jac_1(b)⊆J(b) in the analytic setting.

For divisor-factor extraction, take the common factor g of local generators in the factorial holomorphic local ring. After shrinking, a=g b and V(b) has codimension at least two, or is empty. Multiplication by g^d gives an isomorphism of the graded Rees algebras, so the ordinary and normalized blowups are unchanged. Principalizing g b supplies a common resolution for b and G=div(g). Its divisor coefficients satisfy F_a=F_b+π*G; the multiplier formula and local projection formula give J(a)=g J(b). Thus the valuation difference is unchanged.

For a p-exceptional E, the common blowup is the identity outside V(b). Its center therefore lies in V(b), and m=v(b)>0. The inclusion already proved gives ell≥v(J(b)), so k_E+1≤n(m−ell)≤n(v(a)−v(J(a))). This establishes the stronger bound and therefore the original bound. A nonexceptional divisor maps onto a base divisor whose general point avoids V(b); there the map is an isomorphism and k_E=0. The inclusion a⊆J(a), again immediate from bounded integrands, makes the right-hand side nonnegative. In dimension one every nonzero local ideal is principal, the blowup is the identity, and no exceptional case remains.

Harmless clarifications: adapted center coordinates are chosen at general smooth center points; divisibility x_i=s h_i does not assert order exactly one; and the published [ELSV Theorem 4.2(i)](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~dror/paper-jump.pdf) places its codimension condition on V(J(b)). Here b⊆J(b) implies that condition from codim V(b)≥2. Its algebraic theorem is only a source comparison: the analytic inclusion was reconstructed above. These clarifications require no substantive repair.

This PASS establishes only the stated supporting theorem. It does not establish special Fujita approximation, entropy recovery, slope equality, original catalogue closure, or any equivariant or family extension.
premises: Local analytic principalization: for every nonzero coherent ideal I on a smooth complex manifold M and every point x, after shrinking to a relatively compact coordinate neighborhood U, there is a proper holomorphic modification π:Z→U obtained by finitely many blowups with smooth centers, with Z smooth and I O_Z=O_Z(-F), where F is effective integral and its support together with the exceptional divisors has simple normal crossings. Bierstone–Milman, Desingularization Algorithms I, §§1.3–1.4, Example 1.19(1).

On a smooth complex manifold, for a nonzero coherent ideal I=(f_j), the ordinary exponent-one analytic multiplier ideal J(I) is the coherent ideal of holomorphic germs h for which |h|²/(Σ_j|f_j|²) is locally integrable. On any proper holomorphic log resolution π:Z→U with I O_Z=O_Z(-F), it equals π_*O_Z(K_{Z/U}-F). Demailly, Analytic Methods in Algebraic Geometry, §§5.4–5.9.

For a coherent ideal I on a reduced complex analytic space X whose zero set is nowhere dense, the ordinary analytic blowup is Proj_an,X(⊕_{d≥0} I^d). Its normalization exists as a finite holomorphic map from a normal complex analytic space, is an isomorphism over the regular locus of the ordinary blowup, and the pulled-back ideal on the normalized blowup is invertible. Lejeune-Jalabert–Teissier, Clôture intégrale des idéaux et équisingularité, Proposition 3.2 and §§4.1–4.2.

Every reduced complex analytic space has a dense open regular locus. In a normal complex analytic space the singular locus has codimension at least two. Demailly, Complex Analytic and Differential Geometry, Chapter II, Theorems 5.3 and 7.6.

The local ring of holomorphic germs at a point of a smooth n-dimensional complex manifold, isomorphic to C{x_1,…,x_n}, is a unique factorization domain. Demailly, Complex Analytic and Differential Geometry, Chapter II, Theorem 2.10.
For a proper holomorphic map F:X→Y of complex analytic spaces, F(X) is a closed analytic subset of Y. Demailly, Complex Analytic and Differential Geometry, Chapter II, Theorem 8.8.
